concepts.name: Internal and surface forces
concepts.mechanism: Internal heat and plate motion can deform Earth's crust. Solar energy and gravity power many surface processes. Landforms reflect their interaction with rock, climate and time; the mantle is not a fully liquid ocean.
concepts.example: A mountain belt can rise through tectonics while rivers incise valleys in it. Uplift and erosion can operate together.
concepts.mistake: Uplift does not mean erosion stops; surface change is not explained by one force alone.
items: A rising mountain is also cut by rivers. Which explanation fits?
The mantle must be fully liquid
Which energy source chiefly supports tectonic activity?
Two mountain belts have similar uplift but different rainfall and rocks. Must their valleys develop identically?
No; surface conditions and resistance also matter

concepts.name: Weathering in place
concepts.mechanism: Weathering breaks down or alters rock at its location. Physical weathering fragments it; chemical weathering changes minerals. Root action and organisms can contribute. Removal and transport are separate processes.
concepts.example: Water freezing in a crack can fragment rock. Oxidation can alter iron-bearing minerals. Neither example requires the debris to move downstream.
concepts.mistake: Breaking a rock in place is not the same as carrying its fragments away.
items: A rock cracks while remaining where it formed. This is—
Iron-bearing minerals oxidize in a stationary rock. Which description fits?
What separates weathering from removal by an agent?
Roots widen a crack in a hillside rock; fragments remain beside it. Which evidence would establish subsequent erosion?
An agent detaches and removes fragments
The rock has a different colour

concepts.name: Erosion and its agents
concepts.mechanism: Erosion detaches and removes material through agents such as flowing water, ice, wind or waves. Their importance depends on climate, event intensity, geology and exposure. A desert can experience substantial episodic water erosion; wind is not automatically dominant everywhere.
concepts.example: An intense storm can cut a dry channel in a desert. Strong winds can remove fine loose sediment elsewhere in the same region.
concepts.mistake: A landscape label such as desert does not identify its strongest erosional agent without evidence.
items: A desert channel deepens during a rainstorm. Which agent is directly evidenced?
Wind simply because it is a desert
What information best supports identifying the main erosional agent?
The colour of a textbook map
A dry basin has storm-cut gullies and wind-shaped dunes. What conclusion is justified?
Erosion is impossible in dry places

concepts.name: Sediment transportation
concepts.mechanism: Transportation is the movement of sediment after detachment. Rivers can carry dissolved material, suspended particles and bed load. Flow conditions, particle size, sediment supply and channel geometry affect what can be moved.
concepts.example: Fine silt may remain suspended while larger grains move along the bed. Slower water does not necessarily deposit every particle immediately.
concepts.mistake: Sediment in motion is not deposition, and speed alone does not determine every particle's behaviour.
items: Silt moving downstream in suspension is—
Which pair helps explain whether a river can move a grain?
Which statement distinguishes transport from deposition?
Transport moves material; deposition accumulates it
A flow weakens; fine silt remains suspended while coarse grains settle. Is this possible?
Yes; particles have different settling and transport requirements
No; every grain must settle at once
No; fine silt is always bed load

concepts.name: Conditional deposition
concepts.mechanism: Deposition is settling or accumulation of transported material when conditions favour it. Changes in transport capacity, particle size and the receiving environment matter. A river mouth forms a delta only when sediment accumulation can outpace removal.
concepts.example: A coarse bar can accumulate where flow loses transport capacity. Strong coastal waves may remove enough delivered sediment to limit delta growth.
concepts.mistake: Not every speed decrease deposits every grain, and not every river mouth builds a delta.
items: Sediment settling and accumulating on a river bar is—
A river delivers sediment but waves remove most of it. What can this limit?
Which statement about deposition is best?
It depends on particle and flow/environment conditions
Every grain settles whenever speed falls
It occurs only at river mouths
Two river mouths receive similar loads, but one coast removes sediment much faster. Which outcome is plausible?
The faster-removal coast must accumulate more

concepts.name: Landforms and their evidence
concepts.mechanism: River incision can create valleys; lateral channel movement and deposition can produce floodplains, bars and meanders. Glaciers, wind, waves and dissolution also create landforms. Identify the mechanism from feature evidence rather than assuming every shape has one origin.
concepts.example: A V-shaped valley with active river incision and a U-shaped valley with glacial evidence suggest different dominant shaping histories.
concepts.mistake: Rivers can erode and deposit in several reaches; the upper/middle/lower-course model is a simplification.
items: Repeated overbank sediment accumulation helps build—
A point bar is accumulating beside a migrating channel. Which process is evidenced there?
Why should landform interpretation consider several agents?
Similar forms can have different histories and conditions
Every landform has one universal cause
A valley has a broad U-shaped cross-section and moraines. Which evidence-based explanation should be investigated?
River incision solely because a stream now exists
Wind erosion solely because it is wide
Plate folding solely because it is deep

concepts.name: Slope failure and mass wasting
concepts.mechanism: Mass wasting moves material downslope under gravity. Failure occurs when driving stress exceeds resisting strength. Water can raise pore pressure; slope cuts, geology, vegetation and earthquakes can alter stability. No single factor explains every landslide.
concepts.example: A road cut and intense rain can jointly destabilize a fractured slope. Assessment needs drainage, material strength and exposure evidence.
concepts.mistake: Calling all landslides a result of deforestation ignores water, geology, slope changes and triggers.
items: Downslope movement driven mainly by gravity is—
Rain raises pore-water pressure in a weak slope. What should be assessed?
Whether resisting strength is reduced relative to stress
Which landslide explanation is adequately conditional?
Geology, slope, water and triggers interact
Rain always causes every slope to fail
A vegetated slope fails after excavation and heavy rain. What is the best investigation?
Combined changes in geometry, drainage and strength

concepts.name: Ice, wind, waves and dissolution
concepts.mechanism: Glaciers erode and deposit as ice moves. Wind can remove and deposit loose sediment. Waves and coastal currents reshape shores. Dissolution of suitable rock under appropriate water chemistry can form karst. Each mechanism has conditions and characteristic evidence.
concepts.example: Moraines indicate ice-related deposition; dunes indicate wind transport/deposition; limestone caves may indicate dissolution.
concepts.mistake: A feature's shape alone is insufficient; combine material, setting and process evidence.
items: A moraine is most closely associated with—
A limestone cave develops where water dissolves rock. Which process fits?
Wind regime, sand supply and vegetation
A sheltered coast gains sand while an exposed cliff retreats. What can explain the contrast?
Different wave energy, sediment supply and rock conditions

concepts.name: Settlement on changing landforms
concepts.mechanism: Landforms influence access, agriculture, drainage and settlement, but livelihoods, infrastructure and institutions also matter. Fertile floodplains can attract settlement while remaining exposed to flooding and channel migration.
concepts.example: Two floodplain towns can have different outcomes because housing, warning access and evacuation routes differ despite similar flood depths.
concepts.mistake: Fertile land is not flood-free, and physical geography does not mechanically determine prosperity.
items: Why can floodplains attract settlement despite risk?
Fertile land and access can offer benefits alongside hazards
What should a floodplain building decision examine?
Flood history, drainage, exposure and vulnerability
Does similar relief guarantee similar settlement outcomes?
No; institutions and access also matter
Yes; human decisions have no effect
Yes; climate controls every social outcome
Two towns face similar flood depths but different warning and evacuation access. Must losses be identical?
No; capacity and vulnerability affect outcomes
Yes; hazard depth is the only factor

concepts.name: Basin management and flood risk
concepts.mechanism: Flood risk combines physical hazard with exposure, vulnerability and response capacity. Basin planning, warnings, wetlands, zoning and infrastructure can reduce risk. Embankments and dams can shift risk as well as provide protection; assess upstream and downstream effects.
concepts.example: Protecting one bank with an embankment may alter water levels or exposure elsewhere. Management needs basin-scale evidence and local participation.
concepts.mistake: A protective structure is not proof that all downstream risks or future floods vanish.
items: What should an embankment proposal assess?
Effects on local and downstream risk
Only whether its wall is tall
Whether it removes all sediment forever
Which is a basin-level risk reduction measure?
Coordinated warning, zoning and drainage planning
A barrier protects one settlement but raises water levels near another. How should its success be judged?
Compare distributed benefits, shifted risks and alternatives
Reject every structure regardless of evidence
